lead: This unit is the iOS side of the course: the Swift language, the Xcode toolchain, and the UIKit screens a user actually touches. After it you can write Swift values, functions and classes, build and debug an app, lay out a screen with Auto Layout, show data in table and picker views, and move between screens with segues. One fare calculator — ₹20 base plus ₹9.0 per km — runs through every chapter.
about: The unit has two halves. Chapters 6.1 to 6.3 are the Swift language: constants, variables and data types; then operators, control flow, strings and functions; then structs, classes and inheritance. Chapters 6.4 to 6.8 are the toolchain and the screen: building, running and debugging in Xcode; UIKit and Interface Builder with outlets and actions; then the longest chapter, displaying data through table views, picker views, image views, menus and control events. Chapter 6.7 makes those screens fit every phone with Auto Layout and stack views, and 6.8 joins screens with segues and a navigation controller. A three-trip fare list (₹92, ₹158, ₹65) is computed once and reused in later chapters, so the numbers in the figures always match the text.

chapters.idea: Swift keeps every value in a constant or a variable, and the type of that value decides which operations are legal.
chapters.depth: let for a constant (bound once), var for a variable; naming rules; type inference versus explicit annotation such as let rate: Double = 9.0; the core types Int, Double, Float, Bool, String, Character and tuples. Swift is type-safe and never converts silently, so Double(km) and Int("8") are written by hand. Optionals: Int("eight") is nil, unwrap with if let and the ?? operator. print and string interpolation. Some syllabi file these first lessons under 'SDK lessons' or 'documentation'; only a few universities teach Swift itself as a language unit, so keep this chapter short and move on to real code.

figure.title: Three names, their types and their values
figure.aria: Four memory slots: baseFare holds 20.0, rate holds 9.0, km holds the integer 8, and the computed total holds 92.0.

chapters.example: A city cab charges a fixed ₹20 booking fee plus ₹9.0 per kilometre. Write the Swift for a trip of 8 km and give the total. Answer: let baseFare: Double = 20.0; let rate = 9.0 (inferred Double); var km = 8 (inferred Int); let total = baseFare + Double(km) * rate = 20.0 + 72.0 = 92.0 rupees. The conversion Double(km) is mandatory: km * rate alone fails with 'binary operator * cannot be applied to Int and Double'. Int("8") gives Optional(8) and Int("eight") gives nil.
chapters.trap: Multiplying an Int by a Double and expecting Swift to convert for you — it does not, and it is a compile error, not a warning. The second trap is treating Int("8") as a plain Int when it is an Optional.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2, which compares iOS with the other mobile platforms.
chapters.leave: Operators and loops to 6.2, classes to 6.3, storing values after the app closes to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Operators, control flow, strings and functions are the four tools that turn stored values into behaviour.
chapters.depth: Arithmetic + - * / % (integer remainder), comparison, logical && || !, ranges a...b and a..<b, nil-coalescing ??, ternary ?:. Branching with if/else, guard, and switch — switch takes ranges (case 0...10), a where clause, and does not fall through. Loops: for-in, while, repeat-while. Strings: +, interpolation, count, isEmpty, prefix/suffix, multi-line strings. Functions: parameters, argument labels versus _, default values, inout, returning a tuple. Name closures once as 'functions you pass around' — they return in 6.6 as table view callbacks. Only a few universities teach Swift at this depth.
chapters.example: Write a function fareLabel(km:) that charges ₹9.0 per km for trips up to 10 km and ₹11.5 per km beyond that, on top of a ₹20 base, and returns a label. For 8 km: 8 ≤ 10, so rate is 9.0, fare = 20 + 8 × 9.0 = 92, output Short trip: ₹92. For 12 km: rate is 11.5, fare = 20 + 12 × 11.5 = 158, output Long trip: ₹158.
chapters.trap: Assuming C-like fallthrough in switch — Swift stops at the first match unless you write fallthrough. Also mixing 0...3 (includes 3) with 0..<3 (stops before 3) in loops over an array.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 6.1 — the constants, types and optionals being operated on.
chapters.leave: Methods on types to 6.3, and table view data source callbacks (closures) to 6.6.

chapters.idea: A struct is copied when you assign it; a class is shared by reference, and inheritance lets one class reuse and override another's behaviour.
chapters.depth: Structs: value type, automatic memberwise initializer, mutating methods, stored and computed properties, didSet observers. Classes: reference type, identity with ===, initializers and super.init, override, final, polymorphism, deinit. When to choose which: struct for small model data, class for shared state and for anything the UIKit classes must subclass. Mention that Array, String and Dictionary are structs. Only a few universities teach this — cover the copy-versus-share difference well, the initializer rules lightly.

figure.aria: A Ride base class with two subclasses, Cab which overrides the fare method with a ₹15 booking fee, and Auto which keeps the inherited fare.

chapters.example: Take struct Trip { var km: Int }. Let a = Trip(km: 8) and var b = a; set b.km = 12. Then a.km is still 8 and b.km is 12 — two separate copies. Now take class Ride with func fare(km: Int) -> Double { 20 + Double(km) * 9.0 } and subclass Cab that overrides it to add ₹15. For 8 km, Ride gives 20 + 72 = ₹92 and Cab gives ₹107. If two variables point at one Cab object and one changes it, both see the change.
chapters.trap: Expecting a copied struct to share changes back, and forgetting override or the super.init call in a subclass initializer — both are compile errors students lose marks on.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 6.2 — functions become methods, parameters become initializers.
chapters.leave: UIView and UIViewController subclassing to 6.5; saving model objects to disk to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: An iOS app is compiled, installed on a simulator or device, and inspected while it runs with the debugger.
chapters.depth: Xcode project anatomy: project, target, scheme, bundle identifier, Info.plist, asset catalogue. Build means compile then link; errors, warnings and runtime crashes are three different things. Run on the simulator versus a connected device. Breakpoints, step over and step into, the LLDB console with po, the debug area, the view hierarchy debugger. Reading documentation with Option-click and the built-in developer documentation. Mention the project workflow as edit, build, install, run, debug. Only a few universities teach the tools; exam questions are usually about the order of steps and the meaning of a crash message.
chapters.example: An app stores let fares = [92, 158, 65] and prints each one with for i in 0...fares.count { print(fares[i]) }. The array has 3 items at indices 0, 1 and 2, so the loop reaches i = 3 and the app stops with 'Fatal error: Index out of range'. The debugger pauses on that line and po fares shows the three values. Fix: use 0..<fares.count, or better, for fare in fares.
chapters.trap: Calling a red runtime crash a compile error — a build error stops before install, an index crash happens only when that line runs. Second trap: looping with ... instead of ..< over an array count.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 6.3 — there must be a class or struct worth running.
chapters.leave: Publishing to the App Store to Unit 5, which covers app release for mobile platforms generally.

chapters.idea: UIKit supplies the view classes, a view controller owns one screen, and Interface Builder connects the storyboard to your Swift code through outlets and actions.
chapters.depth: The UIKit layer and its main subclasses; UIViewController and its single view; a storyboard file as a set of scenes, one per view controller; the object library, attributes inspector and assistant editor. Outlets as @IBOutlet weak var of an implicitly unwrapped type, actions as @IBAction func with a sender. View controller life cycle in order: viewDidLoad, viewWillAppear, viewDidAppear, viewWillDisappear, viewDidDisappear, and where setup code belongs. Label, button and text field basics. State that a storyboard is data, not code, and is loaded at run time. Only a few universities teach storyboards; some now use SwiftUI instead.

figure.aria: A UIKit class tree: UIResponder at the root, UIView branching to UIControl and UIButton, and UIViewController branching to the app's own FareViewController.

chapters.example: A screen shows a label reading ₹0 and a button. Tapping the button for an 8 km trip must show ₹92. The code is @IBOutlet weak var fareLabel: UILabel! and @IBAction func showFare(_ sender: UIButton) with the single line fareLabel.text = "₹92" inside. viewDidLoad runs first and is where the outlet is guaranteed to be connected; before that the label is nil.
chapters.trap: Using an outlet from an initializer or from a property observer that fires too early — it is still nil and the app crashes. Another trap: editing the IBAction signature after connecting it, which silently breaks the storyboard connection.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 6.4 — the project must build and run before a screen can appear.
chapters.leave: Full navigation between screens to 6.8; saving user settings to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: A screen shows data by feeding a model array to a view that asks for rows on demand, and by reacting to control events.
chapters.depth: Table views: UITableView with a data source and a delegate, sections and rows, numberOfRowsInSection, cellForRowAt with dequeueReusableCell and a reuse identifier, custom cell classes, didSelectRowAt, reloadData. Picker views: UIPickerView with components and titles. Image views: UIImage, the asset catalogue, contentMode and scaleAspectFit. Menus: UIMenu and UIAction attached to a button or a bar button item — some syllabi call this 'using menus with views'. Control events: switch, slider, segmented control and text field with valueChanged and editingChanged. Additional views: scroll view, stack view, activity indicator, alerts. State the rule that views ask for data; data never pushes into views on its own. Persistence and the file system stay in Unit 4.

figure.title: How one row reaches the screen

chapters.example: Three trips of 8 km, 12 km and 5 km give fares 20 + 8 × 9.0 = 92, 20 + 12 × 11.5 = 158 and 20 + 5 × 9.0 = 65. The table has one section, so numberOfRowsInSection returns 3. In cellForRowAt with indexPath.row = 1 the cell shows ₹158. Tapping that row records index 1 and the next screen must receive 158, not the whole array.
chapters.trap: Using the section where the row belongs, or forgetting that the cell identifier in code must match the one in the storyboard — the app then crashes with 'unable to dequeue a cell'. Second trap: recomputing or re-sorting the array inside cellForRowAt so row numbers no longer match.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 6.2 and 6.5 — functions and closures for the callbacks, outlets for the views.
chapters.leave: Saving preferences and files to Unit 4; the Android equivalents of list and image views to Unit 3; moving to the detail screen to 6.8.

chapters.idea: Auto Layout turns each view's position and size into equations, so one set of rules fits every screen size and both orientations.
chapters.depth: Constraints as equations: leading, trailing, top, bottom, width, height, centerX, centerY; the safe area; intrinsic content size; content hugging and compression resistance priorities (250, 750, 1000); ambiguous versus unsatisfiable layouts and the red lines that report them. Stack views: axis, alignment, distribution fill, fillEqually, equalSpacing, and spacing; nested stacks instead of many hand-made constraints; why fixed frames break after rotation or on a bigger phone. Only a few universities teach constraints at this level — the arithmetic of a fillEqually stack is the examinable part.

figure.title: Width of each button in a fillEqually stack

chapters.example: A horizontal stack view holds three buttons with spacing 8, pinned 16 points from the leading and trailing safe area edges, distribution fillEqually. On a 360-point wide screen: 360 − 16 − 16 = 328 points of content, minus two gaps of 8 = 312, divided by 3 = 104 points per button. On a 320-point screen: 320 − 32 = 288, minus 16 = 272, so each button is 90.67 points.
chapters.trap: Pinning to the view instead of the safe area (content slides under the notch at the top), and giving a label both a fixed width and a trailing constraint — the layout turns ambiguous or unsatisfiable and the fix is to delete one rule, not to shrink fonts.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 6.6 — there must be cells, buttons and labels to constrain.
chapters.leave: Orientation changes on the Android side are in Unit 3, for comparison only.

chapters.idea: A navigation controller keeps a stack of view controllers, and a segue is the storyboard-declared move that pushes one on and passes data across.
chapters.depth: UINavigationController: root view controller, push and pop, the navigation bar and back button, title and large titles. Segue types: show (push inside a navigation controller), present modally, and unwind. Segue identifiers, performSegue(withIdentifier:), and prepare(for:sender:) as the only correct place to hand data to the destination, cast with as? and check for nil. Which life cycle methods run on push and on return (viewWillAppear fires again when you come back). Tab bar controllers as a sibling container that switches between whole stacks — some syllabi list tab bar controllers and the view controller life cycle with this chapter. Only a few universities teach segues; SwiftUI navigation replaces them elsewhere.

figure.aria: The navigation stack with the fare list at the bottom as root and the detail screen for ₹158 pushed on top of it.

chapters.example: The fare list shows rows 92, 158 and 65. Tapping row 1 fires a show segue with identifier showDetail. In prepare(for:sender:) the code reads the selected row as 1, casts segue.destination as? DetailViewController, and sets detail.fare = 158. The stack goes from [Fare List] to [Fare List, Detail]; the back button pops it and the list is unchanged. Presenting the same screen modally instead would leave no back button, only a dismiss action.
chapters.trap: Reading indexPathForSelectedRow inside the destination's viewDidLoad (the selection is gone by then) and force-casting with as! when the identifier or the class is wrong — that crashes instead of doing nothing.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 6.5 and 6.6 — a source screen with data and a destination screen to fill.
chapters.leave: Tab bar controllers beyond one short section, and app publishing to Unit 5.

links: constants and their types are what the operators and functions work on

the classes you write are the code Xcode builds and debugs
